item.title: Nvidia halts shipments of AI servers to four Southeast Asian countries
item.description: Nvidia has asked manufacturing partners to halt server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia following new US export controls on advanced AI chips.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Nvidia has told manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers containing its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, the Financial Times reported on Thursday. The move follows new US curbs that took effect last week, which require export licences for shipments of advanced chips to several Southeast Asian countries. The measures are part of efforts by Washington to shut down routes that Chinese firms are believed to use to obtain advanced AI chips. According to the FT, manufacturing partners such as Dell and Supermicro, which package Nvidia's chips into servers, told buyers in the four countries that Nvidia would not allow their orders to be shipped. It was unclear whether the halt would be temporary as Nvidia and its partners work through compliance requirements under new US export controls, the newspaper said, citing three people familiar with the matter. Nvidia, Dell and Supermicro did not immediately respond to requests for comment outside regular business hours. The Commerce Department published the new rule days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who previously worked at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed. Nvidia's board subsequently reinstated Huang as CEO on November 23. Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner that rents computing power at its data centres, has come under scrutiny for possible illegal diversion of advanced AI chips to China.

item.title: Trump seeks to keep leverage over Xi with 40% China tariff threat
item.description: The US is threatening to raise tariffs on Chinese goods to 40% if trade talks collapse, using the prospect of higher duties to maintain leverage over Beijing.
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Trump seeks to keep leverage over Xi with 40% China tariff threat

Trump seeks to keep leverage over Xi with 40% China tariff threat The US is threatening to raise tariffs on Chinese goods to 40% if trade talks collapse, using the prospect of higher duties to maintain leverage over Beijing.

US President Donald Trump is threatening to double tariffs on Chinese goods to 40% if trade talks collapse, adding fresh tension ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. | Photo: Shutterstock

Bloomberg 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 26 2026 | 11:04 PM IST

Listen to This Article

China vowed to defend its interests after the US unveiled new tariffs on Chinese goods and warned the rate could double if trade talks collapse, injecting fresh tension ahead of a planned meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.   While the new 20% levy remains within the bounds of a trade truce set to expire in January, the threat of a 40% rate - which would kick in if trade talks break down - gives Washington leverage heading into next month's Group of 20 summit, where the two leaders are expected to meet for the fourth time this year.    The US announced the new tariffs on China and other trading partners Wednesday following months of investigations over excess manufacturing capacity. The tariffs are still subject to public comment and could change.

"Partners have been waiting for this shoe to drop for some time," said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute and former Acting Deputy US Trade Representative, adding that the US is using the prospect of higher tariffs as "leverage to secure expected shipments of critical minerals and rare earths, and further purchases of US agricultural goods."   The new duties mark the latest effort by the Trump administration to restore its expansive tariff agenda after the US Supreme Court struck down earlier levies on goods from China and dozens of other economies. The proposal would put China's average effective tariff rate at about 31%, near the level before the ruling, according to Bloomberg Economics estimates.

While bilateral ties are likely to remain stable if the duties stay in the 20% range - a level China has previously indicated it would accept - the 40% threat will color how Beijing responds to US chip curbs and other frictions in the coming weeks as both sides negotiate an extension of the truce. Any miscalculation could quickly complicate talks, particularly with a more hawkish US   Congress pressing for tougher export controls on Beijing.   The US hasn't spelled out exactly what it would take to trigger the more drastic hike on China. A US official, speaking on condition of anonymity ahead of Wednesday's announcement, said the higher rate could kick in if Beijing doesn't comply with a trade deal reached last year.

At a regular briefing Thursday, Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yadong called the US Section 301 investigation that led to the new tariffs "a quintessential act of unilateralism" and urged the two sides to use dialogue to resolve their differences.    Beijing "reserves the right to take necessary measures to resolutely defend its legitimate rights and interests," He added.  In July, the Office of the US Trade Representative announced 12.5% duties on China following a Section 301 investigation into the alleged failure of around 60 economies to prevent forced labor in their supply chains. Tariffs levied under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 are generally seen as more legally durable and flexible than other tools Trump has considered, but they take longer to implement.

"The rate of 20% should be seen as a cap on the two Section 301 investigations," said Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore. "This gives USTR more flexibility to adjust, which is especially useful when there might be a court ruling on forced labor which could ask for changed rates."   Businesses and US states are challenging tariffs over forced labor concerns in court, accusing Trump and US officials of unlawfully using Section 301 to replace earlier tariffs that were either struck down by the US Supreme Court or expired.   The new tariff announcement comes just a week after Trump and Xi met at a gathering of Asia-Pacific economies in Shenzhen. Both leaders appeared to lean heavily on their personal rapport to keep ties between their countries on an even keel, though new strains have emerged surrounding the alleged spy scandal involving Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang, as well as fresh US curbs on offshore chip access for Chinese companies.

item.content:encoded:
Home / Companies / News / Tata Trusts to challenge Chandrasekaran's reappointment in Bombay HC

Tata Trusts to challenge Chandrasekaran's reappointment in Bombay HC The charitable entities controlling the Tata Group are set to challenge N Chandrasekaran's reappointment as Tata Sons chairman

The dispute follows N Chandrasekaran's reappointment as Tata Sons executive chairman for another five years at the September 17 board meeting

Press Trust of India Mumbai 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 26 2026 | 10:40 AM IST

Listen to This Article

The Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and the R.D. Tata Trust (RDTT) will file suits in the Bombay High Court against Tata Sons and six of its directors, challenging the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as executive chairman for a second five-year term. The SDTT will seek ₹50 crore and RDTT will seek ₹15 crore in damages, with 18 per cent annual interest. As per the suits, the September 17 decision to reappoint Chandrasekaran was invalid because it did not receive the affirmative vote required under Article 121 of the company's Articles of Association. The dispute follows N Chandrasekaran's reappointment as Tata Sons executive chairman for another five years at the September 17 board meeting.

The two trusts voted on Wednesday night to pass the resolutions to move HC as there was a lack of any satisfactory replies to the communications sent by them since September 17. Also Read

The immediate relief being sought is to ensure that the chairman during the November 30 meeting is prevented from exercising his casting vote in the event of a split in opinion among nominee directors. Tata Trusts, chaired by Noel Tata, holds around 66 per cent of Tata Sons and has challenged the board resolution passed on September 17. In its September 20 statement, the Trusts said the resolution was not validly passed and had "no legal effect".

At the centre of the dispute are Tata Sons' Articles of Association (AoA) and special rights given to Trusts-nominated directors. It has two nominee directors on its board -- Noel Tata and Venu Srinivasan. On September 17, Noel Tata voted against Chandrasekaran's reappointment, while Venu Srinivasan supported it. As per Trusts, both nominated directors were required to support the decision. In its statement issued in September, the Trusts said the AoA of Tata Sons provide that no decision can be taken unless it has the affirmative support of at least a majority of the Directors nominated by the Tata Trusts. "This is a separate condition under the AoA," it said, pointing out that the AoA does not leave any decision of the board to a mere head count of directors.
